title: Rules for discernment
hookLine: in desolation, don't make big changes

lines: A DECISION THAT LOOKS VERY CLEAR.
cards: It's late, the house is quiet, and everything feels wrong. The job seems pointless. The friendship seems over.

Faith feels hollow. And in that mood a decision shows up, looking very clear: quit, send the message, walk away. In the morning, with coffee and some light through the window, the same choice can look very different.
Ignatius of Loyola wrote a rule for exactly that night, short enough to remember half asleep, and it comes out of yesterday's two words. Today: rules for discernment.

teach.b: Discernment means sorting: telling one thing from another. Back on day six hundred eighty-eight, the first letter of John put it this way: "Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God."
Try them. Test them. Ignatius' rules are a field guide for that testing, and today rests on the fifth.
In time of desolation, he says, never make a change. Stay firm in what you decided before the darkness came, in the calm or in consolation. His reason is plain.
In desolation, the voice giving advice isn't a good counselor, and a decision made in that fog tends to follow the fog. But he doesn't say do nothing.
His next rule says push back against the desolation itself: pray a little more, think it through, look honestly at what's happening, do some small thing against the mood.

teach.h: CHANGE YOUR EFFORT, NOT YOUR PLANS.
teach.b: Change your effort, not your plans.
For the bright days he says: in consolation, think ahead to how you'll be when it passes, and store up strength for then. And stay humble, remembering how little you could manage in the low times.
He also pictures temptation as a commander who studies a fortress and attacks where the wall is weakest. Each person's weak place is different, and knowing your own is part of keeping watch.
None of this means desolation is failure, or that every hard feeling is an enemy. It means some choices deserve daylight, the big ones especially: the job, the move, the vow.
And if the dark ever brings thoughts of harming yourself, that isn't a choice to shelve: call or text 988 in the US, or local emergency help, right away.

how: Ignatian retreat guides and spiritual directors teach the rules for discernment of spirits, and people use them when weighing decisions, often waiting to choose until desolation has passed.

o: a gift for predicting what will happen in the future
sorting inner pulls to tell which ones lead toward God
judging other people's faith to see who is sincere

games.q: testing the spirits — tap the pairs.
p: sorting, telling one thing from another
attacks where the wall is weakest

s: Ignatius says to do nothing in desolation
make no change of plans, but push back on the mood: pray more, look honestly, act against it.
the first letter of John says to try the spirits
"believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God."
Ignatius' rules are only for dark days
he gives advice for bright days too: store up strength, and stay humble.

games.q: you're in desolation. everything feels hollow, and quitting a commitment suddenly looks obvious. what does Ignatius' fifth rule say?
o: act now, while it feels clear.
make no change; hold to what you decided in calm, and push back on the mood.
wait, and do nothing at all.
games.why: never make a change in desolation, he says, but don't just sit there either: pray more, look honestly, act against the mood.

practice: Ask whether there's a choice you've been tempted to make in a low or rattled moment: a message to send, something to quit, a purchase, a door to slam.
Don't decide anything now; set it down gently on a shelf for a calmer day, and notice what it's like to leave it there. If you pray, you can bring it to God and ask for light.

wordCard.voice: Discernment. Sorting the movements inside, testing which pull is which, and choosing in the light.

carryVoice: Your line: never decide in the dark. Morning light can change the whole picture. Until tomorrow.
